A point z₀ where f(z) fails to be analytic, but ∃ a punctured disk 0 < |z - z₀| < R in which f(z) is analytic everywhere.
★ Can be expanded in a Laurent series!
Singularities accumulate! Every neighborhood of z₀ contains infinitely many other singularities.
Example: f(z) = 1 / sin(π/z). Poles at z = 1/n accumulate at z = 0 (non-isolated!).
limᶍ→ᶍ₀ f(z) exists and is finite. Principal part of Laurent series = 0 (NO negative powers!).
limᶍ→ᶍ₀ (z - z₀)ᵐ f(z) = c ≠ 0. Principal part has FINITE negative powers terminating at 1/(z-z₀)ᵐ.
Simple pole if m = 1 | Double pole if m = 2
limᶍ→ᶍ₀ f(z) does not exist (not even ∞). Principal part has INFINITELY many negative powers!
PREPFUSION HALLMARK EXAMPLES FOR EACH CLASS
Residue at z = 0 is EXACTLY ZERO!
Highest negative power is 1/z³ ⇒ POLE ORDER 3!
At z = 0: lim does not exist!
Infinitely many negative powers of z!
Residue = coeff of 1/z = 1! Same for sin(1/z).

R = Distance from expansion center z₀ to NEAREST SINGULARITY of f(z)!
Taylor series has NO negative powers (all powers of (z - z₀) are ≥ 0).
sin z = z - z³/3! + z⁵/5! - ... (|z| < ∞, Entire)
1 / (1 - z) = 1 + z + z² + z³ + ... (|z| < 1, Singular at z = 1)
1 / (1 + z) = 1 - z + z² - z³ + ... (|z| < 1, Singular at z = -1)
ln(1 + z) = z - z²/2 + z³/3 - ... (|z| < 1, Branch cut at z = -1)

LAURENT THEOREM (ANNULAR RING R₁ < |z - z₀| < R₂)
If f(z) is analytic in an open annulus R₁ < |z - z₀| < R₂:
The coefficient b₁ of 1/(z - z₀) in the Laurent series is the RESIDUE!
★ Since ∮ (z-z₀)ⁿ dz = 0 for all n ≠ -1, only b₁ survives contour integration!
Always factor out the dominant variable so the ratio has magnitude < 1:
Only positive powers of z appear (Taylor series).
Only negative powers of z appear (Principal part).
★ The golden rule: Divide by the LARGER quantity so ratio < 1!
THE CANONICAL GATE DRILL: EXPAND f(z) = 1 / [(z - 1)(z - 2)]
f(z) = - ∑ zⁿ / 2ⁿ⁺¹ - ∑ 1 / zⁿ⁺¹ (Both pos & neg powers!)
f(z) = ∑ 2ⁿ / zⁿ⁺¹ - ∑ 1 / zⁿ⁺¹ = ∑ (2ⁿ - 1) / zⁿ⁺¹ (All negative powers)
Principal part has exactly 1 term: -1/(z - 1) ⇒ Residue = -1!
Differentiating between annular rings // Finding b₁ vs b₂ // High-frequency exam traps
TRAP 1: USING THE WRONG ANNULAR EXPANSION
A function does NOT have a unique Laurent series! It has a different series in every annulus.
WHY BLIND EXPANSION FAILS IN GATE:
If question specifies: "Find coefficient of 1/z² for 1 < |z| < 2":
Expanding as 1/(1 - z) instead of (1/z)/(1 - 1/z) gives a DIVERGENT series!
★ Check convergence |ratio| < 1 for EVERY piece of the expansion!
For essential singularities, differentiation formulas CANNOT be used!
Problem: Find residue of f(z) = z³ cos(1/z) at z = 0.
Solved by pure series expansion in 15 seconds without limits!
